'''Willard Sterling Boyle''' (August 19, 1924 – May 7, 2011) was a Canadian applied [[physicist]] who shared one half of the 2009 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] with [[George E. Smith]] for their invention of the [[charge-coupled device]].<ref name="NYT">{{cite news
 |last         = Chang
 |first        = Kenneth
 |date         = October 7, 2009
 |title        = Nobel Awarded for Harnessing Light
 |newspaper    = The New York Times
 |url          = https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/07/science/07nobel.html?_r=1&scp=1&sq=Willard%20Boyle&st=cse
 |access-date  = October 9, 2009
 |archive-url  = https://archive.today/20240526020621/https://www.webcitation.org/696spD3LO?url=http://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/07/science/07nobel.html%3F_r=3&scp=1&sq=Willard%20Boyle&st=cse
 |archive-date = May 26, 2024
 |url-status   = dead
}}</ref><ref name="CBC">
{{cite news
 |date         = October 6, 2009
 |title        = Canadian scientist shares Nobel physics prize
 |publisher    = CBC News
 |url          = https://www.cbc.ca/news/world/canadian-scientist-shares-nobel-physics-prize-1.798175
 |access-date  = September 22, 2015
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20120724010850/http://www.cbc.ca/news/world/story/2009/10/06/nobel-prize-physics-kao-boyle-smith281.html
 |archive-date = July 24, 2012
 |url-status   = live
}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Willard Sterling Boyle was born on August 19, 1924, in [[Amherst, Nova Scotia]], and lived in the nearby village of [[Wallace, Nova Scotia|Wallace]] until the age of three, when he moved with his parents to northern [[Quebec]], where his father worked as a doctor in the logging community. He was homeschooled by his mother, as the nearest school was 30 miles away.<ref name="LA Times Obit">{{cite news
 |last         = Maugh II
 |first        = Thomas H.
 |title        = Nobelist was a father of the digital camera
 |url          = https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2011-may-19-la-me-willard-boyle-20110519-story.html
 |access-date  = July 11, 2012
 |newspaper    = Los Angeles Times
 |date         = May 19, 2011
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20121207190845/http://articles.latimes.com/2011/may/19/local/la-me-willard-boyle-20110519
 |archive-date = December 7, 2012
 |url-status   = live
}}</ref> At age fourteen, he began his formal education at [[Lower Canada College]] in [[Montreal]].<ref name="Nobel bio">{{Cite web|title=Willard S. Boyle – Biographical |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2009/boyle/biographical/|publisher=NobelPrize.org| access-date=November 1, 2026}}</ref>

Boyle attended [[McGill University]], but his education was interrupted in 1943, when he joined the [[Royal Canadian Naval Air Service|Fleet Air Arm]] of the [[Royal Canadian Navy]] during World War II, training to land [[Supermarine Spitfire|Spitfires]] on aircraft carriers.<ref name="Nobel bio"/> After the war ended, Boyle resumed his studies at McGill, where he received a [[Bachelor of Science]] in 1947 and a [[Master of Science]] the following year. In 1950, he received a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in Physics for a thesis on [[mass spectrometry]].<ref name="McGill">
{{cite web
 |title        = McGill congratulates its second Nobel-winning alumnus of 2009
 |work         = Alumni News
 |publisher    = McGill University
 |date         = October 6, 2009
 |url          = https://www.mcgill.ca/newsroom/news/item/?item_id=111171
 |access-date  = October 15, 2009
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20120131050022/http://www.mcgill.ca/newsroom/news/item/?item_id=111171
 |archive-date = January 31, 2012
 |url-status   = dead
}}</ref><ref name="thesis">{{Cite thesis |last=Boyle|first=Willard Sterling |year=1950|title=The construction of a Dempster type mass spectrometer: its use in the measurement of the diffusion rates of certain alkali metals in tungsten |url=https://escholarship.mcgill.ca/concern/theses/xs55mg15b|degree=PhD|publisher=McGill University Libraries|oclc=890947763|id={{ProQuest|301841894}}}}</ref>

== Career ==
After receiving his doctorate, Boyle spent one year at Canada's Radiation Laboratory and two years teaching physics at the [[Royal Military College of Canada]].<ref name="Nobel bio"/>

In 1953, Boyle joined [[Bell Telephone Laboratories]], where he invented the first continuously operating [[ruby laser]] with Don Nelson in 1962. He was made Director of Space Science and Exploratory Studies at Bellcomm (a subsidiary of Bell Labs) in 1962, providing support for the [[Apollo program]] and helping to select lunar landing sites. He returned to Bell Labs in 1964, working on the development of [[integrated circuit]]s.<ref name="McGill"/> Boyle was Executive Director of Research in the Communications Sciences Division from 1975 until his retirement in 1979.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Boyle, Willard S., 1924-2011 |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11412005.html |url-status=live|publisher=American Institute of Physics|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20241212032532/https://history.aip.org/phn/11412005.html|archive-date= December 12, 2024|access-date=November 1, 2026}}</ref>

== Charge-coupled device ==
In 1969, Boyle and [[George E. Smith]] invented the [[charge-coupled device]] (CCD), for which they were jointly awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] in 2009.<ref name="McGill"/> The CCD allowed [[NASA]] to send clear pictures to Earth back from space.<ref name="LA Times Obit" /> It is also the technology that powers many [[digital camera]]s today. Smith said of their invention: "After making the first couple of imaging devices, we knew for certain that chemistry photography was dead."<ref name="Cassingham 2011">{{cite web|url=http://www.honoraryunsubscribe.com/willard_boyle.html|title=Willard Boyle|last=Cassingham|first=Randy|date=May 15, 2011|work=This is True|location=Ridgway, Colorado|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120510164453/http://honoraryunsubscribe.com/willard_boyle.html|archive-date=May 10, 2012|url-status=dead|access-date=July 12, 2012}}</ref> [[Eugene I. Gordon|Eugene Gordon]] and [[Michael Francis Tompsett|Mike Tompsett]], two now-retired colleagues from Bell Labs, claim that its application to photography was not invented by Boyle.<ref>[https://spectrum.ieee.org/nobel-controversy-former-bell-labs-employee-says-he-invented-the-ccd-imager Nobel Controversy: Former Bell Labs Employee Says He Invented the CCD Imager] ''IEEE''</ref>

== Personal life and death ==
In 1946, Boyle married Betty Joyce, with whom he had two sons and two daughters.<ref name="Nobel bio"/><ref name="LA Times Obit"/>

During retirement, Boyle lived in [[Wallace, Nova Scotia]], and in [[Lac Tremblant]], [[Quebec]]. One of his hobbies was sailing his 33-foot boat.<ref name="Nobel bio"/>

Boyle had suffered from [[kidney disease]], and died at a hospital in Wallace on May 7, 2011, at the age of 86.<ref name="LA Times Obit"/>
